sec: AHO, knuckle patterns and calcium treatment

items.q: Which feature is the odd one out for Albright hereditary osteodystrophy?
items.exp: AHO features shortened metacarpals, short stature, round facies and cognitive impairment, not long slender digits. (Book p886)

items.q: The AHO summary emphasizes shortening of the fourth ___ more than the corresponding ___.
items.exp: The handwritten summary states short fourth metacarpal > metatarsal. (Book p886)

items.q: Match the following clenched-fist patterns — 1) Down syndrome 2) Turner syndrome 3) PHP Ia … A) Fourth-knuckle dimple B) Fourth- and fifth-knuckle dimples C) Third-knuckle dimple
items.exp: The diagrams pair Down syndrome with the third metacarpal, Turner syndrome with the fourth and PHP Ia with the fourth and fifth. (Book p886)

items.q: A child with round facies and short stature makes a fist showing 'knuckle, knuckle, dimple, dimple.' Which diagnosis is favored by the illustrated pattern?
items.exp: Fourth- and fifth-metacarpal shortening produces the PHP Ia knuckle pattern in the figure. (Book p886)

items.q: Assess: I A normal clenched fist has a fourth-knuckle dimple. II An isolated fourth-knuckle dimple establishes PHP Ia.
items.exp: The normal diagram shows four knuckles; the Turner diagram also has a fourth-knuckle dimple, so an isolated dimple is not specific for PHP Ia. (Book p886)

items.q: A patient has severe symptomatic acute hypocalcemia with tetany. Which replacement is the chapter's initial intravenous option?
items.exp: The page selects IV 10% calcium gluconate for acute symptomatic disease, rather than the listed oral salts. (Book p886)

items.q: What volume and concentration constitute the chapter's initial calcium gluconate ampoule?
items.exp: The source specifies 10 mL (one ampoule) of 10% calcium gluconate. Its rapid 2–3-minute timing should not be used as an unmonitored clinical protocol; follow ECG-monitored local guidance. (Book p886)

items.q: The continuation regimen printed here places 5 g calcium gluconate in ___ of ___ solution.
items.exp: The source lists 5 g in 500 mL of 5% dextrose, with elemental-calcium dosing separately expressed per kilogram per hour. Do not confuse salt mass with elemental calcium. (Book p886)

items.q: For the source's infusion notation, assess: I The rate is expressed as 1–3 mg elemental calcium/kg/hour. II Five grams of calcium gluconate means five grams of elemental calcium.
items.exp: The page explicitly labels the rate as elemental calcium; the calcium gluconate salt mass is not the elemental calcium mass. A clinical infusion requires monitoring and a validated protocol. (Book p886)

items.q: For acute symptomatic hypocalcemia, which initial calcium gluconate administration best follows monitored clinical guidance rather than the scan’s unusually rapid 2–3-minute line?
opts: 10–20 mL of 10% solution over about 10 minutes with ECG monitoring
10–20 mL of 10% solution as an unmonitored immediate bolus
10–20 mL of 1% solution over about 10 minutes without ECG monitoring
1–2 mL of 10% solution over about 60 minutes with ECG monitoring
items.exp: The source prints 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate over 2–3 minutes, then an infusion over 5 hours. Contemporary product/local guidance uses 10–20 mL of 10% over about 10 minutes with ECG and calcium monitoring; the source timing is not a safe standalone protocol. See the calcium-gluconate SmPC and GGC guideline linked in REPORT_CH36-40.md. (Book p886)

items.q: The page's oral calcium ceiling is ___ per day.
items.exp: Oral calcium up to 2 g/day is the source's adjunct entry; oral therapy is not a replacement for monitored IV treatment of severe symptomatic hypocalcemia. (Book p886)
